name: Maiwala
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Nagai, Yasuko. 1997. Educational change from within: developing a vernacular elementary school in Papua New Guinea. PhD thesis, School of Education, Flinders University of South Australia. xxi+505 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives 9581; open PDF, obtained from an Internet Archive capture of the sil.org file; saved)
catalog_locator: fn. 72, p. 237, sec. 4.5.3 'The Maintenance of the Maiwala Language'; fn. 70, p. 235, sec. 4.5.2; Appendix Four, p. 472.
catalog_quote: The stress is placed on the first vowel and is lengthened [gú:di] to fit the stress pattern of the Maiwala language. [fn. 72, p. 237] ... Almost all the syllables in the Maiwala language are formed by the combination of a consonant and a vowel. The only exception is 'm' final (e.g., tam, malatomtom). Examples of shortened English names are: Kuli from Christopher, Gule from Grace, Dulu from Andrew (stress on the first vowel, and 'r' changed to flapped 'l'); Kobo from Jacob, and Toma from Thomas. [fn. 70, p. 235] ... Moreover, the people shortened it to 'Goody' placing the stress in the beginning according to the stress patterns of the Maiwala language. [Appendix Four, p. 472]
world_status: statement found in an open source

All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators (extracted text, page-by-page): fn.70 on printed p.235 = p.256 ('Almost all the syllables in the Maiwala language are formed by the combination of a consonant and a vowel. The only exception is 'm' final (e.g., tam, malatomtom). Examples of shortened English names are: Kuli from Christopher, Gule from Grace, Dulu from Andrew (stress on the first vowel, and 'r' changed to flapped 'l'); Kob…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nagai, who learned and analysed Maiwala during two years of fieldwork, says the Maiwala stress pattern puts stress on the first vowel (word-beginning), with lengthening of the stressed vowel, and shows English loans being reshaped to fit it (Goody [gú:di], Kuli, Gule, Dulu). Every example is disyllabic, so initial and penultimate stress cannot be told apart; no rule for longer words is given, and this is an education thesis, not a phonological description.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the remarks concern adapted English names and greetings only. Lithgow 1976:475 (cluster-wide, not Maiwala-specific) says stress in Papuan Tip languages shifts one syllable rightward when a kinship noun takes a plural suffix, which would fit a right-edge (penultimate) system rather than a strictly initial one.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (shortened loan names and the greeting 'Goody' as isolated words); the stressed first vowel is also lengthened.
new_statements.identity_note: Nagai's thesis concerns the Maiwala village community (Alotau district, Milne Bay) = Maiwala [mum], Glottolog maiw1249. Lithgow 1976:455 treats Maiwala as a dialect of Taupota (taup1242); Capell 1969:127 and Glottolog/ISO (after the 2001 SIL survey) treat it as a separate language in the Taupota linkage, alongside Wa'ema (waem1237) and Wedau (weda1241). Nagai notes Gabugabuna speakers now speak Maiwala with some Suwau admixture.

Maiwala; Capell 1969:127 had treated Maiwala as a separate language; Ethnologue 2005 split after the 2001 SIL survey). Its phonology chapter covers the Taupota-Wedau chain and explicitly declines to discuss stress (pp.121-122).

sources.citation: Lithgow, David R. 1976. Austronesian languages: Milne Bay and adjacent islands (Milne Bay Province). In Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study vol. 2, 441-523. Pacific Linguistics C-39.
sources.note: p.455 lists Maiwala as a dialect of Taupota (cognate table). Para 84 'STRESS' p.475 is cluster-wide only: vowel lengthening near the end of the phonological word; 'In all of the languages of PTC it seems that stress is predictable within certain word-classes, notably kinship nouns and verbs. When a kinship noun is pluralised by the addition of a suffix, the stress moves one syllable closer to the end of the word'. Nothing Maiwala-specific; no default position.
